situation:
You are to assume the role of corporate partnerships manager at KESTREL FIELDHOUSE, an operator of a downtown arena and event complex that hosts concerts, minor league hockey and trade shows. The chief operating officer (judge) has asked you to recommend how to settle a conflict between two sponsorship agreements before new signage goes up, and to be ready to explain your reasoning.

KESTREL FIELDHOUSE has been profitable for six straight years, and its founder is preparing to hand the company to a new ownership group before the next season opens. Sponsorship is the complex's steadiest revenue and concourse signage is its scarcest asset. The main concourse holds a fixed number of positions, and what sponsors will pay for them has climbed every year as two competing venues opened downtown.

A ten-year agreement with NORTHRIDGE SAVINGS BANK, signed by the founder himself, promises the bank every permanent sign on the main concourse and first refusal on any new asset placed there. Since that agreement was signed, the sales team sold a package to SUMMIT OUTDOOR OUTFITTERS that includes the two new digital boards being installed on that same concourse. Both agreements are in force and the boards go up in six weeks.

Offering the two digital boards to NORTHRIDGE SAVINGS BANK first would honor its first refusal, but the package already sold to SUMMIT OUTDOOR OUTFITTERS would have to be reopened, and the outfitter has said it would not renew. Delivering the boards as sold and offering the bank a substitute package instead would reopen an agreement the founder signed personally and hand the new ownership group a dispute in the middle of the handover.

The chief operating officer (judge) wants you to recommend which agreement gets the boards, what a substitute package of assets would be worth against them, and what the complex should do for the sponsor that is moved. The chief operating officer (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
